claim: Homeostatic and circadian processes collaborate to appropriately time and consolidate sleep and wake.
source: Homeostatic and circadian processes collaborate to appropriately time and consolidate sleep and wake.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract summarizing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Brief sleep deprivation scheduled at different times of day in Drosophila results in elevated morning rebound compared to evening.
source: To understand how these processes are integrated, we scheduled brief sleep deprivation at different times of day in Drosophila and find elevated morning rebound compared to evening.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically the scheduled sleep deprivation experiments.

claim: Time-dependent sleep rebound effects depend on discrete morning and evening clock neurons, independent of their roles in circadian locomotor activity.
source: These effects depend on discrete morning and evening clock neurons, independent of their roles in circadian locomotor activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from genetic manipulations of clock neurons presented in the manuscript.

claim: R5 ellipsoid body neurons show elevated morning expression of activity dependent and presynaptic gene expression.
source: In the R5 ellipsoid body sleep homeostat, we identified elevated morning expression of activity dependent and presynaptic gene expression as well as the presynaptic protein BRUCHPILOT consistent with regulation by clock circuits.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data and immunostaining experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: R5 ellipsoid body neurons show elevated morning expression of the presynaptic protein BRUCHPILOT consistent with regulation by clock circuits.
source: In the R5 ellipsoid body sleep homeostat, we identified elevated morning expression of activity dependent and presynaptic gene expression as well as the presynaptic protein BRUCHPILOT consistent with regulation by clock circuits.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data showing BRP levels at different times of day.

claim: R5 neurons display elevated calcium levels in response to sleep loss in the morning, but not the evening.
source: These neurons also display elevated calcium levels in response to sleep loss in the morning, but not the evening consistent with the observed time-dependent sleep rebound.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging experiments using GCaMP6s presented in the manuscript.

claim: The circadian clock and the sleep homeostat independently regulate sleep according to the two process model.
source: The classic two process model posits that the circadian clock and the sleep homeostat independently regulate sleep (Borbély, 1982; Borbély et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established models in the field.

claim: The circadian process times and consolidates sleep-wake via phased activity changes in central pacemaker neurons.
source: The circadian process, via phased activity changes in central pacemaker neurons, times and consolidates sleep-wake (Patke et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: The homeostatic process promotes sleep length, depth, and amount as a function of the duration and intensity of prior waking experience.
source: The less well-understood homeostatic process, often assayed after extended sleep deprivation, promotes sleep length, depth, and amount as a function of the duration and intensity of prior waking experience (Deboer and Tobler, 2000; Franken et al., 1991; Huber et al., 2004; Werth et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: Sleep homeostasis is thought to be mediated by the accumulation of various wake-dependent factors, such as synaptic strength.
source: Sleep homeostasis is thought to be mediated by the accumulation of various wake-dependent factors, such as synaptic strength (Tononi and Cirelli, 2014), which are subsequently dissipated with sleep.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis.

claim: Homeostatic drive persists in the absence of a functioning circadian clock.
source: While homeostatic drive persists in the absence of a functioning circadian clock (Tobler et al., 1983), homeostatic drive can be modulated by the circadian clock.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Homeostatic drive can be modulated by the circadian clock.
source: While homeostatic drive persists in the absence of a functioning circadian clock (Tobler et al., 1983), homeostatic drive can be modulated by the circadian clock.
evidence: This claim is supported by the context of the manuscript and citations to follow.

claim: Abolishing clock output through mutation of most core clock genes reduces SD-induced changes in NREM sleep.
source: Abolishing clock output through mutation of most core clock genes (Franken et al., 2006; Laposky et al., 2005; Wisor et al., 2002) or electrolytic ablation of the mammalian circadian pacemaker, the suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) (Easton et al., 2004) reduces SD-induced changes in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, an indicator of homeostatic sleep drive in mammals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Electrolytic ablation of the suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) reduces SD-induced changes in NREM sleep.
source: Abolishing clock output through mutation of most core clock genes (Franken et al., 2006; Laposky et al., 2005; Wisor et al., 2002) or electrolytic ablation of the mammalian circadian pacemaker, the suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN) (Easton et al., 2004) reduces SD-induced changes in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, an indicator of homeostatic sleep drive in mammals.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: In forced desynchrony protocols, total time asleep, latency to sleep, and NREM sleep time are reduced in the evening independently of time awake.
source: Under these conditions, a variety of indicators of homeostatic drive such as total time asleep, latency to sleep, and NREM sleep time are reduced in the evening independently of time awake (Dijk and Czeisler, 1994; Dijk and Czeisler, 1995; Dijk and Duffy, 1999; Lazar et al., 2015), consistent with the idea that the clock sustains wakefulness at the end of the waking period in the evening.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: The clock sustains wakefulness at the end of the waking period in the evening.
source: Under these conditions, a variety of indicators of homeostatic drive such as total time asleep, latency to sleep, and NREM sleep time are reduced in the evening independently of time awake (Dijk and Czeisler, 1994; Dijk and Czeisler, 1995; Dijk and Duffy, 1999; Lazar et al., 2015), consistent with the idea that the clock sustains wakefulness at the end of the waking period in the evening.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the cited studies on forced desynchrony.

claim: Drosophila is a well-established model for investigating the molecular and neural basis of circadian rhythms and sleep.
source: To understand the mechanistic basis of circadian regulation of sleep homeostasis, we are using Drosophila, a well-established model for investigating the molecular and neural basis of circadian rhythms and sleep.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Sleep is characterized by quiescence, increased arousal thresholds, changes in neuronal activity, and circadian and homeostatic regulation.
source: Sleep is characterized by quiescence, increased arousal thresholds, changes in neuronal activity, and circadian and homeostatic regulation (Campbell and Tobler, 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Flies display quiescence, increased arousal thresholds, changes in neuronal activity, and circadian and homeostatic regulation.
source: Flies display each of these hallmarks (Hendricks et al., 2000; Shaw et al., 2000; van Alphen et al., 2013) and have simple, well-characterized circadian and sleep neural networks (Dubowy and Sehgal, 2017; Shafer and Keene, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: About 150 central pacemaker neurons express molecular clocks in Drosophila.
source: About 150 central pacemaker neurons that express molecular clocks (Dubowy and Sehgal, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Four small ventral lateral neurons (sLNvs) that express pigment dispersing factor (PDF) are necessary for driving morning activity in anticipation of lights on.
source: Of these, four small ventral lateral neurons (sLNvs) (per hemisphere) that express pigment dispersing factor (PDF) are necessary for driving morning activity in anticipation of lights on and exhibit peak levels of calcium around dawn (~ZT0) (Grima et al., 2004; Liang et al., 2019; Liang et al., 2017; Stoleru et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: PDF+ sLNvs exhibit peak levels of calcium around dawn (~ZT0).
source: Of these, four small ventral lateral neurons (sLNvs) (per hemisphere) that express pigment dispersing factor (PDF) are necessary for driving morning activity in anticipation of lights on and exhibit peak levels of calcium around dawn (~ZT0) (Grima et al., 2004; Liang et al., 2019; Liang et al., 2017; Stoleru et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: The dorsal lateral neurons (LNds) and a 5th PDF- sLNv are necessary for evening anticipation of lights off.
source: The dorsal lateral neurons (LNds) and a 5th PDF- sLNv are necessary for evening anticipation of lights off and show a corresponding evening calcium peak (ZT8-ZT10) (Gossan et al., 2014; Grima et al., 2004; Liang et al., 2019; Liang et al., 2017; Stoleru et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: LNds and the 5th PDF- sLNv show an evening calcium peak (ZT8-ZT10).
source: The dorsal lateral neurons (LNds) and a 5th PDF- sLNv are necessary for evening anticipation of lights off and show a corresponding evening calcium peak (ZT8-ZT10) (Gossan et al., 2014; Grima et al., 2004; Liang et al., 2019; Liang et al., 2017; Stoleru et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Glutamate-positive DN1ps are necessary for morning anticipation.
source: The posterior DN1 (DN1ps) consist of glutamate-positive (Glu+) subsets necessary for morning anticipation and Glu- necessary for evening anticipation under low light conditions (Chatterjee et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Glutamate-negative DN1ps are necessary for evening anticipation under low light conditions.
source: The posterior DN1 (DN1ps) consist of glutamate-positive (Glu+) subsets necessary for morning anticipation and Glu- necessary for evening anticipation under low light conditions (Chatterjee et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Lateral posterior neurons (LPN) are not necessary for anticipation but are uniquely sensitive to temperature cycling.
source: Lateral posterior neurons (LPN) are not necessary for anticipation but are uniquely sensitive to temperature cycling (Miyasako et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: PDF+ large LNv promote wake independently of their clock functions.
source: Specific pacemaker subsets have been linked to wake promotion (PDF+ large LNv (Chung et al., 2009; Parisky et al., 2008; Sheeba et al., 2008), diuretic hormone 31 (DH31+) DN1ps [Kunst et al., 2014]) and sleep promotion (Glu+ DN1ps (Guo et al., 2016), Allostatin A+ LPNs [Ni et al., 2019]), independently of their clock functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: DH31+ DN1ps promote wake independently of their clock functions.
source: Specific pacemaker subsets have been linked to wake promotion (PDF+ large LNv (Chung et al., 2009; Parisky et al., 2008; Sheeba et al., 2008), diuretic hormone 31 (DH31+) DN1ps [Kunst et al., 2014]) and sleep promotion (Glu+ DN1ps (Guo et al., 2016), Allostatin A+ LPNs [Ni et al., 2019]), independently of their clock functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Glu+ DN1ps promote sleep independently of their clock functions.
source: Specific pacemaker subsets have been linked to wake promotion (PDF+ large LNv (Chung et al., 2009; Parisky et al., 2008; Sheeba et al., 2008), diuretic hormone 31 (DH31+) DN1ps [Kunst et al., 2014]) and sleep promotion (Glu+ DN1ps (Guo et al., 2016), Allostatin A+ LPNs [Ni et al., 2019]), independently of their clock functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Allostatin A+ LPNs promote sleep independently of their clock functions.
source: Specific pacemaker subsets have been linked to wake promotion (PDF+ large LNv (Chung et al., 2009; Parisky et al., 2008; Sheeba et al., 2008), diuretic hormone 31 (DH31+) DN1ps [Kunst et al., 2014]) and sleep promotion (Glu+ DN1ps (Guo et al., 2016), Allostatin A+ LPNs [Ni et al., 2019]), independently of their clock functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: The sLNvs and LNds appear to communicate to R5 EB neurons through an intermediate set of dopaminergic PPM3 neurons.
source: The sLNvs and LNds appear to communicate to R5 EB neurons through an intermediate set of dopaminergic PPM3 neurons based largely on correlated calcium oscillations (Liang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work and is based on inference from calcium oscillation data.

claim: The anterior projecting subset of DN1ps provide sleep promoting input to R2/R4M EB neurons via tubercular bulbar (TuBu) interneurons.
source: The anterior projecting subset of DN1ps provide sleep promoting input to other EB neurons (R2/R4M) via tubercular bulbar (TuBu) interneurons (Guo et al., 2018; Lamaze et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Activation of a subset of TuBu neurons synchronizes the activity of the R5 neurons which is important for sleep maintenance.
source: Activation of a subset of these TuBu neurons synchronizes the activity of the R5 neurons which is important for sleep maintenance (Raccuglia et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: The R5 neurons are at the core of sleep homeostasis in Drosophila.
source: Critically, the R5 neurons are at the core of sleep homeostasis in Drosophila (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: R5 neuronal activity is both necessary and sufficient for sleep rebound.
source: R5 neuronal activity is both necessary and sufficient for sleep rebound (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Extended sleep deprivation (12–24 hr) elevates calcium, the critical presynaptic protein BRUCHPILOT (BRP), and action potential firing rates in R5 neurons.
source: Extended sleep deprivation (12–24 hr) elevates calcium, the critical presynaptic protein BRUCHPILOT (BRP), and action potential firing rates in R5 neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by the context of the manuscript and citations to follow.

claim: Knockdown of brp in R5 decreases rebound.
source: The changes in BRP in this region not only reflect increased sleep drive following SD but also knockdown (KD) of brp in R5 decreases rebound (Huang et al., 2020) suggesting it functions directly in regulating sleep homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: BRP functions directly in regulating sleep homeostasis.
source: The changes in BRP in this region not only reflect increased sleep drive following SD but also knockdown (KD) of brp in R5 decreases rebound (Huang et al., 2020) suggesting it functions directly in regulating sleep homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the cited study on brp knockdown.

claim: R5 neurons stimulate downstream neurons in the dorsal fan-shaped body (dFB), which are sufficient to produce sleep.
source: R5 neurons stimulate downstream neurons in the dorsal fan-shaped body (dFB), which are sufficient to produce sleep (Donlea et al., 2014; Donlea et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Flies released into DD following SSD did not exhibit any detectable change in phase.
source: To test if SSD modulated the circadian phase, SSD flies released into constant dark (DD) following the protocol did not exhibit any detectable change in phase (Figure 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: There was no significant difference between total sleep in flies kept in SSD and those under baseline conditions.
source: There was no significant difference between total sleep in flies kept in SSD and those under baseline conditions (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Sleep rebound does not increase over the course of the 7-day protocol.
source: In addition, sleep rebound does not increase over the course of the 7-day protocol further suggesting that flies are able to fully recover sleep during the 4.5 hr rebound period (Figure 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Flies are able to fully recover sleep during the 4.5 hr rebound period.
source: In addition, sleep rebound does not increase over the course of the 7-day protocol further suggesting that flies are able to fully recover sleep during the 4.5 hr rebound period (Figure 1e).
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the observation that sleep rebound does not increase over time.

claim: Wild-type flies display robust rebound in the morning and suppressed rebound in the evening.
source: By comparing flies' baseline sleep to their rebound sleep (sleep after deprivation) around the clock, we observed robust rebound in the morning and suppressed rebound in the evening (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Sleep rebound in the morning is significantly higher than sleep rebound in the evening when controlling for baseline sleep.
source: As indicated in the heat map, we found sleep rebound in the morning is significantly higher than sleep rebound in the evening when controlling for baseline sleep such that there is a>2 x difference in rebound between morning and evening time points (rebound at ZT1.5~133 min and ZT9.5~51 min) (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: There is a significant difference in latency following deprivation between morning and evening.
source: This was also accompanied by a significant difference in latency following deprivation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Elevated rebound in the morning relative to the evening persists under constant darkness (DD).
source: Lastly, we determined if these effects persist under constant darkness (DD). We observed elevated rebound in the morning (CT2.5) relative to the evening (CT10.5), indicating that these differences are not dependent on light (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Morning/evening differences in rebound are not dependent on light.
source: We observed elevated rebound in the morning (CT2.5) relative to the evening (CT10.5), indicating that these differences are not dependent on light (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the observation that differences persist in constant darkness.

claim: Clkout mutants do not display the wild-type morning and evening peaks of wakefulness.
source: In the absence of Clk, flies do not display the wild-type morning and evening peaks of wakefulness and exhibit robust rebound at all times, reaching maximal levels of sleep after each SD (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b (referring to Figure 2d based on context).

claim: Clkout mutants exhibit robust rebound at all times, reaching maximal levels of sleep after each SD.
source: In the absence of Clk, flies do not display the wild-type morning and evening peaks of wakefulness and exhibit robust rebound at all times, reaching maximal levels of sleep after each SD (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Clkout mutants do not exhibit significant differences in rebound between morning and evening time points in LD.
source: Selected morning/evening time points do not exhibit significant differences in rebound in LD (ZT1.5 and ZT9.5) nor in DD (CT2.5 and CT10.5) (Figure 2e and f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Clkout mutants do not exhibit significant differences in rebound between morning and evening time points in DD.
source: Selected morning/evening time points do not exhibit significant differences in rebound in LD (ZT1.5 and ZT9.5) nor in DD (CT2.5 and CT10.5) (Figure 2e and f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: There was no difference in latency between baseline sleep matched morning and evening time points after sleep deprivation in Clkout.
source: There was also no difference in latency between baseline sleep matched morning and evening time points (ZT1.5 and ZT8.5) after sleep deprivation in Clkout (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1e.

claim: pers flies showed elevated rebound in the morning compared to the evening.
source: Similar to wild-type flies, pers showed elevated rebound in the morning compared to the evening; however, as expected, the trough of rebound sleep in the evening was phase advanced relative to wild-type by about 4 hr (ZT5.5 v. ZT9.5) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,c.

claim: The trough of rebound sleep in the evening in pers flies was phase advanced relative to wild-type by about 4 hr.
source: Similar to wild-type flies, pers showed elevated rebound in the morning compared to the evening; however, as expected, the trough of rebound sleep in the evening was phase advanced relative to wild-type by about 4 hr (ZT5.5 v. ZT9.5) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b,c.

claim: pers flies exhibit an increased sleep latency following deprivation in earlier evening time points (ZT7.5) relative to control (ZT9.5).
source: Furthermore, pers flies exhibit an increased sleep latency following deprivation in earlier evening time points (ZT7.5) relative to control (ZT9.5) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c (referring to 1f based on context).

claim: Ablation of most pacemaker neurons using cry39-Gal4 substantially reduced both morning and evening anticipation in males.
source: Ablation of most of the pacemaker neurons including those underlying morning and evening behavior using cry39-Gal4 (Klarsfeld et al., 2004; Picot et al., 2007) substantially reduced both morning and evening anticipation in males (Table 1) as previously described (Stoleru et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1 and citations to published work.

claim: Ablation using cry39-Gal4 abolished the difference between baseline sleep matched morning and evening rebound.
source: Consistent with the loss of circadian function, ablation also abolished the difference between baseline sleep matched morning and evening rebound (Figure 3a and b), displaying high rebound across time points (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a and b.

claim: Ablation of PDF+ neurons using pdf-Gal4 substantially reduced morning anticipation in males.
source: We ablated PDF+ neurons using pdf-Gal4, which we verified by observing substantially reduced morning anticipation in males validating our reagent (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: Ablation of PDF+ neurons still resulted in substantially higher rebound in the morning (ZT1.5) versus the evening (ZT9.5).
source: Nonetheless we still observed substantially higher rebound in the morning (ZT1.5) versus the evening (ZT9.5) (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Ablation of most clock cells except PDF+ neurons using cry39-Gal4 with pdf-Gal80 results in high rebound across time points.
source: Coupling cry39-Gal4 with pdf-Gal80 to ablate most clock cells except PDF+ neurons confirms this observation; these flies display high rebound across time points (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d) and comparably high rebound in baseline sleep matched morning and evening time points similar to cry39-Gal4 (Figure 3d), highlighting the role of non-PDF clock neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d and Figure 3d.

claim: Non-PDF clock neurons play a role in time-dependent sleep rebound.
source: Coupling cry39-Gal4 with pdf-Gal80 to ablate most clock cells except PDF+ neurons confirms this observation; these flies display high rebound across time points (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d) and comparably high rebound in baseline sleep matched morning and evening time points similar to cry39-Gal4 (Figure 3d), highlighting the role of non-PDF clock neurons.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The split Gal4 line R51H05 AD; R18H11 DBD results in expression in just 6–7 neurons per hemisphere with little or no expression elsewhere in the brain.
source: This intersection resulted in expression in just 6–7 neurons per hemisphere with little or no expression elsewhere in the brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations of the split Gal4 expression pattern.

claim: Glu+ DN1p neurons show presynaptic projections to both the pars intercerebralis (PI) and the lateral posterior neuropil.
source: Selective labeling of dendritic and axonal arbors using DenMark (Nicolaï et al., 2010) and synaptotagmin GFP (Zhang et al., 2002), respectively, demonstrated that these neurons show presynaptic projections to both the pars intercerebralis(PI) and more modestly to the lateral posterior neuropil (Figure 4a–c), the latter consistent with a previous report (Lamaze et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a–c and a citation to published work.

claim: Ablation of Glu+ DN1p using the split Gal4 reduced morning anticipation in males.
source: We targeted hid expression using this split Gal4, we observed a reduction in morning anticipation in males demonstrating the necessity of this defined neuronal group (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: Ablation of Glu+ DN1p did not result in significant changes in baseline sleep levels.
source: We also did not observe significant changes in baseline sleep levels (Figure 4g).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: Ablation of Glu+ DN1p suppressed the difference in morning and evening rebound.
source: Despite the lack of a significant change in their baseline sleep/activity profiles, ablation suppressed the difference in morning and evening rebound observed in both Gal4 and hid controls, although there was still a trend towards a morning-evening difference (Figure 4h–j).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4h–j.

claim: Glu+ DN1ps may mediate differences between morning and evening rebound largely independent of their role in regulating baseline sleep/activity.
source: Overall, this indicates that Glu+ DN1ps may mediate differences between morning and evening rebound largely independent of their role in regulating baseline sleep/activity.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing effects on rebound without baseline changes.

claim: Silencing of TuBu neurons using R52B02>Kir eliminated the difference in rebound between morning and evening time points.
source: We used this line in combination with Kir2.1 and found that the difference between morning and evening rebound was lost, similar to what was observed after Glu+ DN1p ablation (Figure 5b, c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b, c.

claim: Knockdown of mGluR in TuBu neurons eliminated the difference in rebound between morning and evening time points.
source: We knocked down the expression of a metabotropic glutamate receptor (mGluR) in these neurons using RNAi (Guo et al., 2016) and observed phenotypes very similar to silencing them (Figure 5d and e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d and e.

claim: Silencing R2/R4m neurons with Kir2.1 eliminated the difference in rebound between morning and evening time points.
source: Silencing these neurons with Kir2.1 eliminated the difference in rebound between baseline sleep matched morning and evening time points, phenocopying TuBu silencing (Figure 5f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5f.

claim: The DN1p-Tubu-R2/R4m circuit plays a role in regulating time-dependent sleep rebound.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate a role for the DN1p-Tubu-R2/R4m circuit in regulating time-dependent sleep rebound.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the experimental results on this circuit.

claim: Ablation of 2–3 LNds and the 5th sLNv using MB122B split Gal4 resulted in high rebound across time points.
source: This manipulation resulted in high rebound across time points in SSD (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a,b) similar to what was observed in Clkout mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a,b.

claim: Ablation of 2–3 LNds and the 5th sLNv abolished the difference in sleep gain between baseline sleep matched morning and evening time points.
source: Furthermore, the difference in sleep gain between baseline sleep matched morning and evening time points was abolished (Figure 6a–c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6a–c.

claim: Ablation of 2–3 LNds and the 5th sLNv resulted in a large increase in rebound in the evening.
source: This effect appears to be due to a large (two- to sixfold) increase in rebound in the evening (Figure 6d), with a more modest(~1.5-fold) effect in the morning (Figure 6e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Ablation of 2–3 LNds and the 5th sLNv did not result in significant effects on anticipation or baseline sleep levels.
source: Surprisingly, we did not observe significant effects on anticipation (Figure 6f–g; Figure 6—figure supplement 2c,d) or baseline sleep levels by ablation (Figure 6i) or silencing (Figure 6—figure supplement 2e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6f–g, Figure 6i, and Figure 6—figure supplement 2c,d,e.

claim: Just 4 PDF- LNd/sLNv cells are essential for clock control of rebound with an especially strong suppressive effect in the evening.
source: Thus, just 4 PDF- LNd/sLNv cells are essential for clock control of rebound with an especially strong suppressive effect in the evening.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the experimental results on LNd/sLNv ablation.

claim: Blocking synaptic transmission in PPM3 neurons reduced the difference in rebound between baseline sleep matched morning and evening time points.
source: However, whie PPM3 silencing did reduce the difference in rebound between baseline sleep matched morning and the evening time points (Figure 7c and d), this effect appears to be due to dramatically reducing rebound in both the morning and evening (Figure 7—figure supplement 2a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7c and d.

claim: PPM3 silencing dramatically reduced rebound in both the morning and evening.
source: However, whie PPM3 silencing did reduce the difference in rebound between baseline sleep matched morning and the evening time points (Figure 7c and d), this effect appears to be due to dramatically reducing rebound in both the morning and evening (Figure 7—figure supplement 2a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2a,b.

claim: Blocking R5 synaptic output reduced rebound in both morning and evening.
source: Blocking R5 synaptic output also reduced rebound in both morning and evening (Figure 7—figure supplement 2a,b), consistent with the role of these neurons in mediating rebound from 12 hr SD terminating in the morning (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2a,b and a citation to published work.

claim: Blocking R5 synaptic output resulted in no difference between baseline sleep matched morning and evening rebound.
source: Moreover, no difference between baseline sleep matched morning and evening rebound was evident (Figure 7e and f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7e and f.

claim: Blocking synaptic output from the dFB reduced rebound at both morning and evening time points.
source: Rebound at both morning and evening time points was reduced (Figure 7—figure supplement 2a,b) similar to what was reported for rebound beginning in the morning (Qian et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2a,b and a citation to published work.

claim: Blocking synaptic output from the dFB resulted in no difference in rebound between baseline sleep matched morning/evening time points.
source: This too resulted in no difference in rebound between baseline sleep matched morning/evening time points as it was for PPM3 and R5 (Figure 7g and h).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7g and h.

claim: Neither morning nor evening SD had much of an effect on gene expression in the R5 neurons.
source: We were surprised to find that neither morning nor evening SD had much of an effect on gene expression in the R5 neurons (Figure 8a and b).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 8a and b.

claim: In the morning, only two genes were significantly differentially expressed (q<0.1, Hsp70Bb and stv) in response to SD.
source: In the morning, only two genes were significantly differentially expressed (q<0.1, Hsp70Bb and stv).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data.

claim: In the evening, only four genes were significantly differentially expressed (q<0.1, CG5522, CG13285, mt:ND5, and Hsp70Bb) in response to SD.
source: Likewise, in the evening, only four genes were significantly differentially expressed (q<0.1, CG5522, CG13285, mt:ND5, and Hsp70Bb).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data.

claim: Comparisons of morning and evening timepoints produce 46–128 differentially expressed genes (q<0.1).
source: In stark contrast, comparisons of morning and evening timepoints with or without sleep deprivation (Morning Control (MC) vs Evening Control (EC), Morning SD (MSD) vs Evening SD (ESD), or MC +MSD vs EC +ESD) produces 46–128 differentially expressed genes (q<0.1, Figure 8c, d and e).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 8c, d and e.

claim: Time-of-day dependent regulation in R5 neurons does not appear to be driven by core clock genes in these neurons.
source: Notably, this time-of-day dependent regulation does not appear to be driven by core clock genes in these neurons (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Clk is detected in only 2 out of 12 samples and only at very low levels in R5 neurons.
source: Clk is detected in only 2 out of 12 samples and only at very low levels in those samples with the expression of other clock genes like per and tim not fluctuating between the two timepoints.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data.

claim: Major active zone regulators such as Syx1A, Rim, unc-104, Srpk79D, and nSyb are all significantly upregulated in the morning.
source: Indeed, major active zone regulators such as Syx1A, Rim, unc-104, Srpk79D, and nSyb are all significantly upregulated in the morning (Figure 8e and f).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 8e and f.

claim: Genes involved in ionic transport across the plasma membrane, including para and CG5890, are significantly upregulated in the morning.
source: We also observed significant upregulation of genes involved in ionic transport across the plasma membrane, including para, a voltage-gated sodium channel (Catterall, 2000; Loughney et al., 1989), and CG5890, a predicted potassium channel-interacting protein (KChIP) (Figure 8e and g).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 8e and g.

claim: Two sodium:potassium/calcium antiporters, CG1090 and Nckx30C, were upregulated in the morning.
source: Two sodium:potassium/calcium antiporters, CG1090 and Nckx30C, were also upregulated (Figure 8e and g).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 8e and g.

claim: Six activity-regulated genes (sr, Cdc7, CG8910, CG14186, CG17778, hr38) were amongst the most significantly upregulated genes in the morning.
source: Amongst the most significantly upregulated genes in our dataset, we found six genes that were previously identified as activity-regulated genes in Drosophila (ARGs; sr, Cdc7 (also known as l(1)G0148), CG8910, CG14186, CG17778, hr38) (Figure 8e and h).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 8e and h.

claim: Several critical components of Creb signaling were enriched in the morning in R5 neurons.
source: Finally, we found that several critical components of Creb signaling were enriched in the morning in R5 neurons (Figure 8e and i).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 8e and i.

claim: CrebA was the most significantly upregulated gene in the morning samples.
source: CrebA was the most significantly upregulated gene in the morning samples, though we also saw significant increases in meng, which encodes a kinase that works synergistically with the catalytic subunits of PKA to phosphorylate and stabilize CREBB (Lee et al., 2018), as well as both regulatory subunits of PKA (Pka-R1, Pka-R2) (Figure 8e and i).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data shown in Figure 8e and i.

claim: BRP levels are higher at ZT1.5 than ZT 9.5.
source: We examined BRP at ZT1.5 and ZT9.5 with and without SD and found that BRP levels are higher at ZT1.5 than ZT 9.5 (Figure 9a and b).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 9a and b.

claim: 2.5 hr SD had no effect on BRP intensity at either ZT1.5 or ZT9.5.
source: Interestingly, 2.5 hr SD had no effect on BRP intensity at either time point (Figure 9b).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 9b.

claim: There was no significant difference in BRP levels between ZT1.5 and ZT9.5 in the Clkout mutant background.
source: We next tested the same two time points in the Clkout mutant background and found no significant difference between ZT1.5 and ZT9.5 (Figure 9b).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 9b.

claim: There was no difference in normalized GCaMP6s signaling between baseline morning (ZT1.5) and evening (ZT9.5) time points.
source: Interestingly there was no difference between the non-SD flies at each time point (Figure 9c).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 9c.

claim: An SD induced increase in calcium was observed in the morning but suppressed in the evening.
source: Nonetheless, an SD induced increase in calcium was observed in the morning but suppressed in the evening (Figure 9c), suggesting that the R5 sensitivity to sleep deprivation is gated by the clock.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 9c.

claim: The R5 sensitivity to sleep deprivation is gated by the clock.
source: Nonetheless, an SD induced increase in calcium was observed in the morning but suppressed in the evening (Figure 9c), suggesting that the R5 sensitivity to sleep deprivation is gated by the clock.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the calcium imaging data.

claim: Discrete populations of the circadian clock network program the R5 sleep homeostat to control the homeostatic response to sleep loss.
source: Here, we describe the neural circuit and molecular mechanisms by which discrete populations of the circadian clock network program the R5 sleep homeostat to control the homeostatic response to sleep loss.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Homeostatic rebound is significantly higher in the morning than in the evening.
source: Using this strategy, we demonstrated that homeostatic rebound is significantly higher in the morning than in the evening.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Distinct subsets of the circadian clock network and their downstream neural targets mediate the enhancement and suppression of morning and evening rebound respectively.
source: We then identified distinct subsets of the circadian clock network and their downstream neural targets that mediate the enhancement and suppression of morning and evening rebound respectively.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Homeostatic drive in the R5 neurons is stored post-transcriptionally.
source: Our studies suggest that homeostatic drive in the R5 neurons is stored post-transcriptionally.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the RNA-sequencing data showing minimal transcriptional changes in response to SD.

claim: The percent of sleep lost recovered at ZT0 with 2.5 hr SD is close to 100% versus 14–35% seen in 12 hr SD protocols.
source: Here, we demonstrate that shorter 2.5 hr deprivations not only induce a robust rebound sleep response (Figure 2), but also the percent of sleep lost recovered at ZT0 is close to 100% versus 14–35% seen in 12 hr SD protocols (Blum et al., 2021; Kayser et al., 2014; Nall and Sehgal, 2013; Oh et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to published work.

claim: Many effects observed in R5 neurons with 12 hr SD (e.g. increased BRP and upregulation of nmdar subunits) are no longer observed with shorter SD.
source: Using this shorter SD, we now find that many effects observed in R5 neurons with 12 hr SD (e.g. increased BRP and upregulation of nmdar subunits) are no longer observed with shorter SD, even though the necessity of R5 neurons for rebound is retained after 2.5 hr SD (Figure 7e and f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The necessity of R5 neurons for rebound is retained after 2.5 hr SD.
source: Using this shorter SD, we now find that many effects observed in R5 neurons with 12 hr SD (e.g. increased BRP and upregulation of nmdar subunits) are no longer observed with shorter SD, even though the necessity of R5 neurons for rebound is retained after 2.5 hr SD (Figure 7e and f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7e and f.

claim: Reduced BRP expression in the R5 reduces rebound.
source: As reduced BRP expression in the R5 reduces rebound (Huang et al., 2020), it is possible that clock-dependent changes in expression of BRP and associated presynaptic modifications are driving the difference in rebound observed in morning/evening.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Clock-dependent changes in expression of BRP and associated presynaptic modifications may be driving the difference in rebound observed in morning/evening.
source: As reduced BRP expression in the R5 reduces rebound (Huang et al., 2020), it is possible that clock-dependent changes in expression of BRP and associated presynaptic modifications are driving the difference in rebound observed in morning/evening.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the observed data and cited work.

claim: The proposed roles of the DN1p and LNd clock neurons are sleep and wake promotion consistent with findings after sleep deprivation.
source: Of note, the proposed roles of the DN1p and LNd clock neurons are sleep (Guo et al., 2016) and wake promotion (Guo et al., 2018) consistent with our findings after sleep deprivation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work and the experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: By using chronic silencing methods, baseline effects may not be evident due to compensatory changes but these effects are only revealed when the system is challenged by sleep deprivation.
source: We hypothesize that by using chronic silencing methods, baseline effects may not be evident due to compensatory changes but that these effects are only revealed when the system is challenged by sleep deprivation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the experimental observations.

claim: A major role of these clock neuron subsets may be to manage homeostatic responses.
source: Nonetheless, the finding of sleep homeostasis phenotypes in the absence of significant baseline effects suggests that a major role of these clock neuron subsets may be to manage homeostatic responses.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Circadian and homeostatic processes do not compete for influence on a downstream neural target but the circadian clock programs the homeostat itself.
source: Our studies suggest that circadian and homeostatic processes do not compete for influence on a downstream neural target but that the circadian clock programs the homeostat itself.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Elevated BRP in the morning is the opposite of what would be expected based on a sleep-dependent reduction in BRP proposed by the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis.
source: It is notable that elevated BRP in the morning is the opposite of what would be expected based on a sleep-dependent reduction in BRP proposed by the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis (Tononi and Cirelli, 2014), suggesting a sleep-wake independent mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and comparison to the synaptic homeostasis hypothesis.

claim: Baseline transcriptomic changes underlie the differential R5 sensitivity to sleep deprivation evident as calcium increases in the morning and not the evening.
source: We hypothesize that these baseline transcriptomic changes underlie the differential R5 sensitivity to sleep deprivation is evident as calcium increases in the morning and not the evening.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the experimental observations.

claim: Transcriptomic and proteomic studies of the mouse forebrain across time and after sleep deprivation are consistent with the model that the circadian clock programs the transcriptome while homeostatic process function post-transcriptionally.
source: Indeed, trancriptomic and proteomic studies of the mouse forebrain across time and after sleep deprivation are consistent with the model that the circadian clock programs the transcriptome while homeostatic process function post-trranscriptionally (Brüning et al., 2019; Noya et al., 2019), paralleling what we have found for R5.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work and comparison to the current findings.
